clue.text: Spirits kept up by this chicken at feeding time?

definitions.meaning: 'keep your ... up' is a British idiom meaning stay cheerful, so this keeps spirits up
a hen at feeding time is busy pecking at grain

explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep your pecker up' is old British slang for keeping your spirits up; the second sense is simply a bird that pecks.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the idiom for courage or cheer; the other is a bird that pecks its food.

clue.text: How some would arrange an away match

definitions.text: How some would arrange an away match

parts.words: How some would arrange an away match
parts.note: a match is a marriage, and arranging it away from home means running off secretly to wed

explanation.walkthrough: 'away match' suggests a sports fixture; the match is a marriage made by running away.
explanation.definitionFit: Couples who run off secretly to marry arrange their wedding away from family.

clue.text: An English miss should be some 60 per cent better than this

definitions.text: An English miss should be some 60 per cent better than this

parts.words: An English miss should be some 60 per cent better than this
parts.note: the proverb says a miss is as good as a mile, and an English mile is about 1.6 of the metric unit

explanation.walkthrough: 'A miss is as good as a mile' makes the miss a mile; a mile is about 60 per cent longer than the metric distance. 'English miss' poses as a girl.
explanation.definitionFit: The metric distance is roughly five-eighths of a mile, so a mile beats it by about sixty per cent.

clue.text: A river rising in Victoria

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means the letters are read upwards, backwards

parts.note: the Niger is a West African river

explanation.surface: A river has its source somewhere in Victoria.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising' turns A NIGER upwards; Victoria is the queen, not the Australian state.
explanation.definitionFit: Queen Victoria signed herself Victoria R, the R standing for the Latin for queen.

clue.text: Yesterday's war engine is today's window-breaker

definitions.meaning: a siege machine hurling stones at walls in ancient warfare
a boy's forked sling with elastic, used to fire stones at panes

explanation.walkthrough: The same word names the ancient siege machine and the modern child's slingshot.
explanation.definitionFit: The name covers both the medieval stone-throwing siege engine and the schoolboy's elastic slingshot.

clue.text: Bath murder. Apple-dish, a little rope — yes, clues' to the killer

parts.note: an apple charlotte is a baked pudding
a cord is a thin rope
aye, also spelt ay, means yes

explanation.surface: A murder-mystery: an apple pudding, a scrap of rope and a 'yes' are the clues to who did it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bath murder' sets the scene: Marat was stabbed in his bath in 1793 by this Frenchwoman.
explanation.definitionFit: She assassinated the revolutionary Marat in his bath, so she is that murder's perpetrator.

clue.text: Actor has first-class comeback in the country

indicators.note: 'has' says the country takes in a changed version of first-class in place of its own letters

parts.note: Spain is a country

indicators.note: a comeback is a return, so the first-class letters are read backwards

parts.note: A1 means first-class, written AI

explanation.surface: A performer makes a fine return to the stage in his homeland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comeback' turns AI (A1) into IA, which replaces the AI in THE SPAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Thespis was the legendary first Greek actor, so a thespian is a performer on stage.

clue.text: The governor, or his heavy artillery ?

definitions.text: The governor, or his heavy artillery

parts.words: The governor, or his heavy artillery
parts.note: an Ottoman provincial ruler, who was himself one of the big guns, a person of great importance

explanation.walkthrough: An Ottoman governor was a 'big gun', so the man is his own heavy artillery.
explanation.definitionFit: A pasha was a high-ranking Ottoman governor, and an important figure is called a big gun.

clue.text: Babel 18's break up one gun in the combat area

indicators.note: 'in' puts the rearranged letters inside the combat area

parts.note: the lists were the enclosed ground for jousting
I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: breaking something up scatters its letters into a new order

explanation.surface: Breaking up one gun on the battlefield.
explanation.walkthrough: 'break up' scrambles one and gun, and 'in' sets them within the medieval jousting ground. The page prints 'Babel 18's'; the 18 looks like a stray mark and plays no part.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tower of Babel produced many tongues, a crowd of speakers of languages.

clue.text: Like a seat of learning giving pass to member, one before tea perhaps

indicators.note: one is placed ahead of what follows in the answer

parts.note: a col is a mountain pass
a leg is a limb, a member of the body
I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: 'perhaps' says the letters of tea could be arranged differently

explanation.surface: Something academic seems to involve handing a pass to a member just before afternoon tea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' turns TEA into ATE; COL + LEG + I + ATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Collegiate describes things belonging to or organised like a college, a seat of learning.

clue.text: George's castle material

definitions.meaning: George ... was the pen name of the French novelist Aurore Dupin, so this is George's surname
children build castles on the beach from this

explanation.walkthrough: George Sand was the pseudonym of a 19th-century French woman novelist; the second sense is a beach sandcastle.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the novelist George's surname and the stuff beach castles are built from.

clue.text: It's the start of the air-trip, too

definitions.text: It's the start of the air-trip, too

parts.words: It's the start of the air-trip, too
parts.note: a word that normally means an end point is also the name for the building where a flight journey begins

explanation.walkthrough: The italic 'start' marks the paradox: the word means an end, yet an air passenger's journey begins at one.
explanation.definitionFit: An air passenger's trip begins at the airport building of this name, though the word usually means a finishing point.

clue.text: A ten-up variety of butter

indicators.note: a variety is a different form, so the letters of 'A ten-up' take a new arrangement

explanation.surface: An odd brand of butter is being advertised as 'ten-up'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'variety of' rearranges A TEN UP; the answer names a kind of butter.
explanation.definitionFit: Peanut butter is a familiar spread, so the nut names a type of butter.

clue.text: Bob and Tom's style of singing

parts.note: a bob was a shilling in old British money, abbreviated s
a tom is a male cat

explanation.surface: Two men named Bob and Tom have a distinctive way of singing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bob' was slang for the old British shilling, written s.; 'Tom' is a tomcat. The names look like two singers.
explanation.definitionFit: Scat is jazz singing using improvised nonsense syllables instead of words.

clue.text: Young Reynard's snuggery

parts.note: Reynard is the traditional fox, his young is a cub, and a snug little den sounds like a place it lives by

explanation.walkthrough: Reynard is the fox of fable; his young is a cub, so a cub's snug hole is a small cosy room.
explanation.definitionFit: A small snug room or recess sounds like a den a fox cub would curl up in.

clue.text: Brother ! You don't say !

definitions.meaning: a monk of a Cistercian order is addressed as Brother
read literally, a description of someone who keeps a vow of silence

explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation 'You don't say!' is read literally: members of this monastic order are known for keeping silence.
explanation.definitionFit: A Trappist is a monk of a strict Cistercian order famed for its vow of silence.

clue.text: The Elephant's Child was a tidy one

definitions.text: The Elephant's Child was a tidy one

parts.words: The Elephant's Child was a tidy one
parts.note: Kipling's Just So story of the curious young elephant; a tidy one means a sizeable thick-skinned beast

explanation.walkthrough: 'The Elephant's Child' is Kipling's Just So story; 'tidy' means considerable, not neat.
explanation.definitionFit: Elephants are classed as thick-skinned beasts, so a young elephant is a large one of these.

clue.text: Most nearly vertical, the sword put up between good men

indicators.note: 'between' places the sword inside the two good men

parts.note: good men are saints, abbreviated ST, here two of them

indicators.note: in a down clue put up means read upwards, reversed

parts.note: an epee is a fencing sword

explanation.surface: The sword is raised between two good men in the steepest climb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up' turns the fencing sword upwards, as a down answer reads; 'between' sets it between two saints, the good men.
explanation.definitionFit: The steepest slope is the one closest to vertical.

clue.text: A worker sent inside — the Invisible Man ?

indicators.note: 'inside' says the word sent goes within the other pieces

parts.note: a worker is a bee, the commonest crossword worker

explanation.surface: A labourer has been locked up, so he is the man nobody sees any more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside' looks like prison slang for a jailed labourer, but it simply places the word within the others.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is away is not seen, so a missing person is an invisible man.

clue.text: A bit hard on the nail

definitions.text: A bit hard on the nail

parts.words: A bit hard on the nail
parts.note: combines two money idioms: 'hard' money in coin and paying 'on the nail', meaning at once

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard cash' is coin or notes, and 'cash on the nail' means paid on the spot; the surface suggests a hammer blow.
explanation.definitionFit: Ready money is called hard when it is coin and is paid 'on the nail' when paid immediately.

clue.text: Goggled at what the Pied Piper does up here

indicators.note: in a down clue 'up' reads the letters from bottom to top

parts.note: the Pied Piper cleared Hamelin of rats, so he derats

explanation.surface: People goggled at the Pied Piper performing his trick in this place.
explanation.walkthrough: The Pied Piper derats Hamelin; 'up here' turns DERATS upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To goggle is to gaze wide-eyed, as one does when one stared.

clue.text: Chessman out of work, we hear, or inversely Percy

indicators.note: 'we hear' says the letters are a word that sounds like the result

parts.note: a bishop is a chessman; out of work removes OP, the usual abbreviation for a work

explanation.surface: A chess player has lost his job, and we hear he is called Percy, or the other way round.
explanation.walkthrough: BISHOP loses OP (work), giving BISH, which is said like the answer. 'or inversely' notes that the poet's names run Percy then this one, so the answer sits after Percy.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet Shelley was christened Percy Bysshe, so this is Percy's companion name.

clue.text: Is French 10 so black ?

definitions.meaning: in heraldry ... is the colour black

explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference points to SAND at 10 across; the French for sand is this word, which is also heraldic black.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the French word for beach grit and the heraldic term for black.

clue.text: A fringe definition of the "Not at home " deception

parts.note: someone not at home is out
lying is deception

explanation.surface: Saying you are 'not at home' to visitors is a fib, here given a marginal definition.
explanation.walkthrough: Telling a caller you are 'not at home' when you are is lying, so the phrase builds OUT + LYING.
explanation.definitionFit: Outlying places are remote, on the edge or margin of a district.

clue.text: Fates of one or two Poles

parts.note: one Pole, here north, N
taken as written
both poles, north and south, N and S

explanation.surface: The destinies of one or two Polish people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' are the magnetic poles, not Polish people: one pole (N), OR, two poles (NS).
explanation.definitionFit: The Norns are the three goddesses of destiny in Norse myth.

clue.text: Robert eats many a banger

indicators.note: eating takes something inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: Bob is short for Robert
M, the Roman numeral for a thousand, stands for many

explanation.surface: A man called Robert tucks into many sausages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banger' looks like a sausage (British slang) but means something that goes bang.
explanation.definitionFit: A bomb goes off with a loud bang, so it is a banger.

clue.text: Wine playfully laced with arsenic

parts.note: alludes to the comedy 'Arsenic and Old Lace', in which two sweet old ladies poison guests with a homemade wine

explanation.walkthrough: In the play and film 'Arsenic and Old Lace' the aunts poison lonely gentlemen with this homemade wine; 'playfully' points to the play.
explanation.definitionFit: The aunts in the black comedy serve poisoned wine made from the fruit of the elder tree.

clue.text: Of late, without money one has to be dependent

indicators.note: 'without' in its old sense of outside puts one piece round the money

parts.note: to rely on something is to be dependent on it
a cent is a coin, a unit of money

explanation.surface: Lately anyone without money finds they must depend on others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' is used in its old sense of outside, not lacking.
explanation.definitionFit: Lately and in the recent past both mean of late.

clue.text: Leasehold grant to start semi-detached construction
